# randomPlantedForest

<!-- badges: start -->
[![R-CMD-check](https://github.com/PlantedML/randomPlantedForest/actions/workflows/R-CMD-check.yaml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/PlantedML/randomPlantedForest/actions/workflows/R-CMD-check.yaml)
[![Codecov test coverage](https://codecov.io/gh/PlantedML/randomPlantedForest/graph/badge.svg)](https://app.codecov.io/gh/PlantedML/randomPlantedForest)
[![randomPlantedForest status badge](https://plantedml.r-universe.dev/badges/randomPlantedForest)](https://plantedml.r-universe.dev/randomPlantedForest)
<!-- badges: end -->

`randomPlantedForest` implements Random Planted Forest ([Hiabu, Mammen & Meyer][arxiv1]), a tree ensemble whose predictions you can read off directly.
The explanation is exact and is not a post-hoc approximation.

The fitted model is a short sum of main effects and interactions.
Interactions of order three or higher are simplified such that they can be displayed as the sum of a limited number (`max_panels`) of heat maps; often without loss in accuracy.

```{r lead-data, include = FALSE}
library(randomPlantedForest)
library(glex)
library(ggplot2)
library(patchwork)

set.seed(1)
n <- 1000
sim <- data.frame(x1 = runif(n, -1, 1), x2 = runif(n, -1, 1), x3 = runif(n, -1, 1), x4 = runif(n, -1, 1))
sim$y <- 1 + sin(pi * sim$x1) + 2 * (sim$x2^2 - 1 / 3) + sim$x3 / 2 + 2 * sim$x1 * sim$x2 +
  rnorm(n, sd = 0.3)
```

```{r lead-fit, include = FALSE}
model <- rpf(y ~ ., data = sim)
```

```{r lead-figure, echo = FALSE, fig.width = 6, fig.height = 5.2, fig.alt = "The four components of a fitted model: three curves and one heat map, with the true functions drawn over the curves."}
comp <- predict_components(model, sim)
truth <- function(f) {
  geom_line(aes(x, y), data = data.frame(x = seq(-1, 1, 0.01), y = f(seq(-1, 1, 0.01))),
            inherit.aes = FALSE, colour = "orange", linewidth = 0.8)
}
panels <- (autoplot(comp, "x1") + truth(function(x) sin(pi * x))) +
  (autoplot(comp, "x2") + truth(function(x) 2 * (x^2 - 1 / 3))) +
  (autoplot(comp, "x3") + truth(function(x) x / 2)) +
  autoplot(comp, c("x1", "x2")) +
  plot_annotation(
    title = sprintf("prediction = %.2f + m(x1) + m(x2) + m(x3) + m(x1, x2)", comp$intercept),
    subtitle = "fitted components (dark) and the true functions (orange)"
  )
panels & theme(text = element_text(size = 12))
```

The figure shows a model fitted to simulated data,
$$y = 1 + \sin(\pi x_1) + 2(x_2^2 - 1/3) + x_3/2 + 2x_1x_2 + \text{noise},$$
with a fourth predictor `x4` that has no effect.
The model found the four true components and nothing else, in one call:

```r
model <- rpf(y ~ ., data = sim)
```

## Why use it

- **Interpretability & Accuracy**
   A random planted forest can be fully visualized and provides state-of-the-art accuracy. By default the fit prunes irrelevant terms such that the fit is easier to comprehend and only keeps relevant terms.

-  **No tuning needed**
While some parameters can be changed, random planted forest works very well in its default settings and needs no tuning.

- **Instead of a GAM or GA²M.**
  - You do not specify the interactions: the forest finds which pairs and triples matter.
  - Smoothness is not assumed.

- **When it does not fit.**
  - Outcomes driven by interactions of many predictors (images, text)
  - Data too large (if memory or computational time is an issue one can reduce the number of families `n_families` and the maximal order of interaction `max_interaction`; usually at the cost of some accuracy)
  - Complex data (work in progress): e.g. time series, dependent rows, survival data etc.

## What the default does

A plain `rpf(y ~ ., data)` takes three steps, each with its own switch:

1. **Grow** 200 tree families of up to three-way interactions, choosing the number of splits out of bag while they grow (`n_splits = NULL`).
2. **Prune** the forest's components to those that matter, with the rule and threshold chosen out of bag (`prune = TRUE`).
3. **Simplify**: every kept three-way component is coarsened such that it can be visualized as the sum of at most 10 heat maps, and the model is pruned again (`max_panels = 10`).

## Installation

From [r-universe][r-universe]:

```r
install.packages("randomPlantedForest", repos = "https://plantedml.r-universe.dev")
```

or from [GitHub](https://github.com/PlantedML/randomPlantedForest):

```r
# install.packages("pak")
pak::pak("PlantedML/randomPlantedForest")
```

## Regression

Ozone in New York, from daily temperature, wind and sunlight:

```{r airquality}
library(randomPlantedForest)

air <- na.omit(airquality)
set.seed(1)
ozone <- rpf(Ozone ~ ., data = air)
ozone
```

`predict()` returns a tibble, and `predict_components()` the components, which add up to it:

```{r airquality-predict}
predict(ozone, head(air, 3))
head(predict_components(ozone, head(air, 3))$m)
```

## Classification

```{r penguins}
penguins <- na.omit(palmerpenguins::penguins)
set.seed(1)
by_sex <- rpf(sex ~ ., data = penguins)
predict(by_sex, head(penguins, 3))
```
